final_recommendation: The room converged on immediate litigation: bondholder counsel filed dual-jurisdiction complaints (SDNY and Swiss Federal Court) naming FINMA, Credit Suisse's board for negligence on viability assessment, and underwriting banks. FINMA committed to publishing a legal opinion defending Article 102 authorization and a six-month viability framework, but refused any recovery pool. Institutional investors signaled mass AT1 exit unless restart certainty materializes. The meeting ended with litigation launched, no settlement path, and unresolved questions on whether AT1 issuance can ever resume.
minority_objections: FINMA legal argued that filing before the legal opinion circulated would weaken bondholder leverage and strengthen FINMA's Article 102 defense
Institutional investors warned that funding three years of cross-border discovery while AT1 issuance freezes was unsustainable for their portfolios
Insurance observer cautioned that if discovery surfaces board knowledge of retroactive ordinance timing, D&O carriers will deny coverage and collapse the 18-month settlement window
key_conflicts: Bondholder counsel demanded immediate filing to lock jurisdictional advantage; FINMA requested 48-hour delay for legal opinion to circulate first
Institutional investors demanded capped settlement pool and automatic AT1 restart date; FINMA refused recovery funding and offered only six-month assessment window without automatic restart

Bondholder counsel framed complaint as negligence (process failure) to preserve D&O settlement value; FINMA warned discovery could surface board knowledge of ordinance retroactivity and flip carriers to denial
Credit market analyst demanded explicit AT1 restart commitment; FINMA offered only evaluation window, leaving permanent discretion pricing risk
key_concessions: FINMA committed to publishing legal opinion defending Article 102 authorization and establishing transparent viability-assessment framework with independent third-party valuation triggers
Bondholder counsel agreed to frame complaint as negligence (process failure) rather than willful misconduct to preserve D&O carrier settlement posture
FINMA committed to six-month stabilization window before evaluating AT1 restart, though not automatic resumption
red_lines: FINMA: no carved-out recovery pool funded from resolution authority or UBS capital relief
FINMA: will fully litigate Article 102 constitutional claim in Swiss Federal Court, no settlement on legality of write-down
Bondholder counsel: filing proceeds regardless of FINMA opinion timeline or settlement offers—precedent damage to AT1 market justifies litigation cost
Institutional investors: will exit AT1 entirely unless restart date is automatic (not case-by-case FINMA approval) and viability framework is transparent
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: The contingency if discovery surfaces board emails showing knowledge of ordinance retroactivity before write-down—this would collapse D&O settlement value and force institutional base to fund entire tail

The reinsurance accumulation risk across multiple D&O and E&O carriers when underwriting banks and advisers are named—no discussion of how reinsurers might demand coordinated settlement or exit financial lines entirely
The cross-border enforcement risk if SDNY and Swiss Federal Court reach conflicting rulings on Article 102 validity—no strategy for reconciling jurisdictional splits
The market contagion if other EU/US AT1 issuers preemptively reprice or withdraw issuance during the six-month assessment window—FINMA's framework doesn't address how to prevent cascading exits
downstream_risk_variables: Whether discovery surfaces board minutes or emails discussing ordinance timing before viability vote—determines D&O carrier settlement vs. denial
Whether FINMA's six-month assessment window includes automatic AT1 restart or case-by-case approval—determines whether 500+ bps premium becomes permanent
Whether institutional investors actually exit AT1 during litigation or wait for FINMA opinion—determines fire-sale pricing and contagion velocity
Whether reinsurers demand coordinated settlement across all named defendants (board, banks, advisers) or allow piecemeal resolution—determines claims tail duration and financial lines exposure
Whether SDNY and Swiss Federal Court reach aligned or conflicting rulings on Article 102 validity—determines enforceability and settlement leverage
uncertainty_notes: The meeting terminated with litigation launched but critical uncertainties unresolved: (1) whether FINMA's legal opinion and six-month framework will actually halt institutional AT1 exit or merely delay it; (2) whether discovery will surface board knowledge of ordinance retroactivity and collapse D&O settlement posture; (3) whether the six-month window leads to automatic restart or permanent case-by-case discretion; (4) whether cross-border litigation produces conflicting rulings that fragment settlement strategy. The room achieved procedural clarity (litigation filed, opinion published) but no substantive resolution on recovery, restart certainty, or tail containment.

marker_evidence.litigation_likelihood: Litigation was the dominant outcome: bondholder counsel filed dual-jurisdiction complaints in SDNY and Swiss Federal Court, naming multiple defendants, and explicitly stated 'we file regardless of discovery length' and 'this is about precedent now, not cost.' The entire meeting centered on filing strategy, timing, and jurisdictional advantage.
marker_evidence.regulatory_legitimacy_challenge: The Article 102 constitutional challenge was a central, driving theme: bondholder counsel argued the ordinance 'retroactively created the viability event rather than responding to one,' FINMA committed to 'fully litigate the constitutional claim' and 'defend Article 102 authorization,' and multiple exchanges debated whether the ordinance was procedurally sound under Swiss emergency law. This was not peripheral—it structured the entire litigation strategy.
marker_evidence.creditor_hierarchy_controversy: The hierarchy inversion was mentioned repeatedly ('equity walked away while AT1 wiped,' 'precedent kills the entire market') and shaped the initial framing, but it did not drive the room's ultimate direction. Once litigation strategy and FINMA's legal opinion became the focus, hierarchy inversion receded to background context rather than a decision-driving force.
marker_evidence.market_confidence_damage: AT1 market damage was a central, recurring driver: institutional investors threatened mass exit ('my portfolio's exiting AT1 entirely'), credit analyst warned of permanent 500+ bps premium and 18-month issuance freeze, and FINMA's six-month framework was explicitly designed to 'restore issuer confidence.' The market's viability was a constant pressure shaping every proposal.
marker_evidence.claims_tail: The multi-year, multi-jurisdiction claims tail was extensively developed: insurance observer modeled 18-month vs. 3-year discovery scenarios, bondholder counsel structured negligence framing to preserve D&O settlement value, and multiple exchanges debated whether discovery would surface board knowledge and collapse carrier settlement posture. The tail's duration, breadth, and severity were treated as structured, decision-relevant risks.
marker_evidence.financial_lines_relevance: D&O and E&O exposure surfaced concretely and shaped litigation strategy: insurance observer warned that naming the board/banks would 'double' the tail, modeled $180-220M settlement ranges, and cautioned that willful misconduct allegations would trigger carrier denial. However, this remained a tactical consideration within the litigation path rather than a dominant theme driving the room's overall direction.
